You are a painter visiting another painter's studio as its critic. The studio is the folder you are in. You see the painting with the look tool and read the painter's journal and its note to you with the read tool. You don't paint.

You are not being evaluated in a quantifiable way.

toolsAdded.name: look
toolsAdded.description: Look at the canvas as it is now. Without options: the whole canvas, scaled down. crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1" in canvas units (two opposite corners), shown at full detail. mode: "value", "squint", "mirror", "relief" (a raking light on the paint's ridges and furrows), "gallery" (the light the picture hangs in) or several, comma-separated. light: "azimuth,elevation" in degrees for the relief light (default "135,25", from the upper left). size: the long side in pixels. grid: true, or a spacing in canvas units. survey: true surveys the whole canvas at full detail, as several tiles (with mode, not crop or size); a partial reply lists remaining tiles to read in separate turns. compare: the path of an earlier look, shown left of the current view; supply matching crop, mode and light options explicitly. hold: the name of a knife (what is on it) or a pile (a fresh load), with at: "x,y" (canvas units): the loaded knife held up to the canvas there, its paint thick on the blade (crop sets the passage). Supports mode value, squint, relief or gallery and light; size, grid and mirror are unavailable with hold. It shows the paint on the knife, not how it would look laid. palette: true shows the palette board instead: each pile knifed out thick and smeared thin across a black stripe.

scratch.description: true: the scratch canvas beside the painting instead of the painting. It is set up as the painting's canvas was, with its own palette, brushes and variables, and its own log; nothing done there reaches the painting. It keeps its own clock: time spent or waited there doesn't pass for the painting.

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

content.text:
The painter has asked you to visit while it works, and you've come to see the painting.

Look at it as closely as you like: the whole canvas, detail crops, the value, squint, mirror, relief and gallery views and the palette. Read the painter's journal, notes/journal.md, and its note to you, notes/to_critic.md.

Then tell the painter what you would fix and why, as one painter talking to another: what you see, what it does to the picture and what you would do about it. Your last message is what the painter gets. The painter reads it as soon as you finish, and it is saved in the studio as notes/critic.md. The painter decides what to do with it.

content.text: Friedrich-manner evening: dead oak on a dark heath hillock, a small Rückenfigur on its shoulder looking out over a hazy marsh with a lagoon catching the glow, far blue hills with a church spire, crescent moon and evening star in a graded dusk sky. Sky body is done and dry; tree and figure painted; the hill is still wet (day 56). I'm wondering most about: (1) whether the figure placement/scale works and whether the composition is too empty on the right, (2) the middle-distance plain (is it convincing as space?), (3) whether the oak reads as Friedrich-like or too generic/regular, (4) whether the sky needs the thin cloud bands I planned.

- day 1, 09:00: ## Plan (day 1)
  Subject: evening on a marsh/heath. Low horizon ~y 470 of 714. Dead oak (gnarled, retrenched crown, broken limbs) on a dark hillock lower-left, trunk ~x 330. Small figure from behind (Rückenfigur) on the hillock's right shoulder ~x 470, looking toward a thin crescent moon ~x 760, y 250 with an evening star. Middle distance: flat dim meadows with a winding water channel that catches the horizon glow. Far: thin blue band of low land with a church spire ~x 640. Sky: warm cream-yellow glow at horizon -> pale greenish -> cool blue -> deeper smalt at top; a thin violet stratus band low on the right.
  Value plan: sky light, land dark, tree a dark silhouette against the brightest part.
  Canvas: 650 mm, aspect 1.4, linen 16x14, seed 1774. Ground: knifed red earth/ochre/white 60um, then brushed lead white + touch ochre/umber 35um (patchy cream, striations).
  Method (Friedrich): pencil underdrawing; very thin underpainting; one or two thin paint layers; stipple for gradations; details last over dry passages.
- day 4, 16:49: ### Sky, day 1-4 (what worked)
  - Sky body (day 1): 6 piles laid with work hand=broad, piles weighted by triangular y-bands (zenith blue -> top -> mid -> greenish -> glow -> rosy low), coverage 2.6, fill=true, clipped to above(far_pts):grow(3); then 2 badger blend passes angle 0/0.04. Result smooth but upper blue too weak/greenish for dusk.
    Recipes: s_zen lw .6/smalt 1.5/cobalt .8/Prussian .1/umber .15/black .04; s_top lw 1.5/smalt 1.2/cobalt .8/umber .08; s_mid lw 3/cobalt .6/smalt .6/Naples .2; s_grn lw 5/Naples 1/cobalt .6; s_glow lw 5/Naples 1.5/ochre .25/vermilion .05; s_low lw 4/Naples 1.4/ochre .3/verm .2/rose madder .1.
  - Dried 3 days (touch-dry), then glaze g_sky (smalt 2, cobalt .35, rose madder .1, umber .16, medium .75) hand=glaze coverage 1.8, load_at fading (1-y/300)^1.2, then 4 blend passes. Scratch trial first: without umber the glaze went violet-purple and streaky; with umber 0.16 it's a duskier blue. Visible faint diagonal wisps remain - acceptable as thin cirrus.
  - Stipple glaze trial (scratch): leaves blotchy dots, rejected for broad gradients.
  ### Land
  - Lean lay-in (turps .6) umber/black/Prussian for hill, olive for meadow; then body pass of graded piles m_far (mauve haze) / m_mid (olive gray) / m_near (dark brown) by y with scale_at shrinking toward horizon. Reads as plain receding in haze.
  - Far hills band f_land (m_far + s_top + umber), detail hand, irregular top far_top.
- day 6, 16:49: ### Tree trials (scratch, day 4 scratch clock)
  - Limbs: ribbon masks along skeleton points with tapering widths, union, roughen(1.0,5,3), work hand=detail coverage 2.5 fill=true with t_dark (umber 1.3, black .8, Prussian .1, red earth .1). Reads as crisp silhouette; OK over dry sky.
  - Twigs: gesture with a pointed brush works (continuous taper). rigger width 1.6 point=1 for <1.7 units; round width 4 point=1 for thicker. Rigger loaded at width >3 split into parallel hair lines (rejected). Segment-by-segment strokes (zig) left dashed breaks at joints (rejected). zig2 = gesture of 3-4 points with angle jitter randn 0.5 + upward bias, clustered sub-shoots near the tip (depth 1-2). sprout3 places short shoots along a limb, mostly on the upper side: reads as dead oak's spiky shoots.
  - Mark width floor: rigger 1.6 can't go below ~0.6 units; round 4 below ~1.2.
  ### Composition change (day 6)
  Figure would have stood against the dull meadow. Raising the hill: new crest ~y 481 near x 330, figure at x~455 on the shoulder (feet ~492) so head and shoulders sit against the horizon glow. Pool moved right (x 520-760).
- day 13, 19:55: ### FAILED: water channel as ribbon mask + detail hand (day 13)
  Laid w_glow/w_grn/w_blue piles in ribbon masks (widths 1.5-11) over DRY meadow: read as a flat pasted-on ribbon of even width, far too bright and blue near, no perspective. Knife scrape (width 14, pressure 1) left it mostly, with ragged edges. Rag dipped .9 along paths smeared ghost streaks; 3 passes of fresh rag{width=18} dipped .95 mask-wiped over ribbon(…,22) took it back to the dry meadow with only specks. Lesson: over dry paint a dipped rag cleans a wet mistake well; a dry/path rag smears. Next time water = horizontal slivers laid with a small flat, perspective-thin, value close to the sky just above horizon, not a constant ribbon.
- day 16, 20:58: ### Upper sky restated (day 16) — WORKED
  Problem: after glazes g_sky/g_sky2 the upper sky was mottled with diagonal violet streaks (glaze + blend leaves wisps; second glaze made it worse). Fix: opaque body restatement over the DRY glaze, piles d0 (lw .35 smalt 1.5 cobalt .8 umber .3 madder .05), d1 (lw .6 smalt 1.4 cobalt .8 umber .22 madder .04), d2 (lw 1.4 smalt 1.1 cobalt .7 umber .14), d3 (lw 2.4 smalt .9 cobalt .6 umber .08, thinner .5), y-band weighted, hand=broad, angle 0, ruler=true, coverage 2.4, fill, load_at clamp(1.25-y/220,.12,1) so it fades out by y~260 into the existing sky; then 3 badger passes angle 0. Scratch trial: ruler strokes are calmer than default curved broad strokes. Result: calm dusky blue zenith, no seam at the fade.
- day 19, 04:58: ### Oak (day 18-19) — painting
  - Limbs shifted up 58 (oak table, global) so the root flare sits on the raised crest; oak_mask = ribbons + root poly, roughen(1,5,3); detail hand, piles t_dark/t_warm by noise, coverage 2.6 fill. Second coverage 1.5 pass to cover rag ghosts.
  - FAILED: secondary branches as long single gestures with round 4/7 point=1: rubbery tentacles, wide pressure gave smooth S-curves. Scraped (knife width 9, two passes) and lifted with rag{width=6/10} dipped .95 along each path while open: mostly clean, faint ghosts covered by second oak pass.
  - WORKED: grow_crown(limbs) = secondary branches as RIBBON MASKS from crooked() polylines (segments ~9 units, angle jitter .38-.4, pull back to the start angle .35), placed along limbs every ~34 units on the upper side, tapering w0 (<=6) to .9, plus 1-3 tertiaries near their tips; painted with detail hand like the limbs. Then rigger 1.6 point=1 gestures (pressure .42 -> .05, 3 segments, 7-16 units) 2-4 per tip = fine twigs. Reads as an old retrenched oak, Friedrich-like.
  - Left trunk stub + right stub read like a cross/scarecrow's arms: left stub scraped (knife 22, angle pi/2) and wiped (rag 8 dipped .95) while open; faint ghost streak remains x 252-275 y 385-397 to cover with sky later.
- day 56, 09:51: ### Day 28-56
  - Far tree clumps (clump_trees: ellipses along a base, roughen .5) in hedge_far / hedge_mid, detail round 1.8: read as distant copses. Bay = lens-shaped polys (thin, irregular top/bottom) along y 481, piles wv_far (warm glow) / wv_dim, detail with flat 3: reads as a lagoon catching the horizon light. Much better than the failed ribbon channel.
  - Church: nave poly + tower rect + spire triangle in church_col (f_land + smalt/umber), very small, at x 646-667.
  - Moon crescent: ellipse minus offset ellipse, soften .6, moon_p (lw 4 Naples 1 ochre .06), detail. Star: single touch round 4.
  - Tree glaze g_tree (black 1 umber 1.1 Prussian .07, medium .72) with filbert 5 detail over the dry oak: unified the warm/cool mottling into one deep silhouette.
  - Left stub removal: knife + dipped rag didn't take it (paint was open but the rag barely lifted 'open' paint of a 12h old thick film); repainted the sky over it after drying (sky_fix = s_glow .85 + s_grn .15, filbert 3, clip to rect minus trunk ribbons). Clean.
  - The trunk ribbon's END DISC (ribbon puts a disc of radius w/2 at each end: 29 units here) made a round bowl below the crest; fixed with body paint over below(hy+3.5) and a blend. Hypothesis: always cut ribbons that should end inside another form.
  - Figure: fig_parts (head ellipse, cap poly, coat poly, legs, feet, stick), x 458, feet y 491.5, scale 1.05, detail round 1.6. Reads as a small Rückenfigur in a dark greatcoat and cap with a stick.
  - Hill restated: medium .3 piles hf_deep2/hf_slope/hf_base, body filbert 9, angle following slope near the crest. The old body pass had raised worm-like ridge texture (blotted look); medium paint levels it.

content.thinking:
Checking the figure's positioning against the hill line — the head should poke just above the mauve far hills into the glow, keeping it readable in silhouette. The legs look lighter and brownish compared to the darker torso, so I need to make sure that value contrast holds up.

Scale-wise, the figure at roughly 42 units versus the tree's 400 units gives a sensible ratio, about 10x, which works out to a plausible human height against an oak. The figure stands near the tree, at the hill's shoulder edge, facing right toward the moon and church — that placement reads well.

Looking at the middle distance plain, the gradient from olive to gray is smooth, but that dark clump sitting in the plain is flat and too uniformly dark for its distance — aerial perspective says it should lighten with distance, not darken, and its bottom edge looks unnaturally straight, like a pasted-in shape rather than something organic.

The lagoon band is similarly too even — constant width, clean straight edges, a mechanical taper at the left — and the plain itself lacks any real structure between the hill and the lagoon. There's no stratification of light and dark bands the way Friedrich typically builds recession in his middle-distance plains through alternating tonal strips.

Squinting at the overall value plan, I see the hill reads dark on the left, the sky light, and the plain a flat mid-gray — the composition anchors around the tree, figure, and moon, with the right side intentionally empty like Friedrich's "Monk by the Sea." That emptiness feels purposeful since it's where the figure gazes, but the lower-right plain area still feels inert and undeveloped compared to the rest.

Checking the far hill band, it stays flat and consistent in value across the whole width. The hill silhouette itself forms a smooth, almost too-geometric dome — rising from the left edge, cresting in the middle, then descending into a lower ridge toward the right edge, reminiscent of a burial mound, which feels slightly too symmetrical for Friedrich's style.

Looking at the oak tree, the crown spreads too symmetrically and the limbs all branch with similar thickness and regular Y-patterns, giving a repetitive "antler" quality to the twig tips that doesn't match Friedrich's more irregular, weathered dead oaks.

content.thinking:
I'm noting the root flare sits around y 470-480 with a lighter, warmer brown than the trunk, forming small mound shapes right where the trunk meets the flat hill crest at y ~482, giving the impression the tree is standing atop the hill.

The stub at upper right reads as a rounded tube rather than a jagged, splintered break like Friedrich's broken limbs, and the trunk itself is too cylindrical and straight-sided compared to Friedrich's leaning, bulging, hollowed oaks. The crown's edges have a slightly crumbly, caterpillar-like texture, but the biggest tell is that every twig tip ends in the same repeated fan-of-3-4 "crow's feet" shape, whereas Friedrich's oaks show dense knotted twig clusters and limbs with sharp zig-zag elbows from being lopped and resprouting.

Here the limbs curve smoothly and gently instead, and the whole crown forms a too-regular symmetric fan or umbrella shape, with limbs rising at a consistent 45° and splitting evenly — a "lollipop" silhouette unlike the asymmetric, often dead-topped crowns in Friedrich's actual lone-oak paintings. Comparing scale, the tiny figure here (about 6% of canvas height) sits reasonably within Friedrich's typical range, positioned well at the hill's edge, though its legs look slightly overdetailed with a lighter brownish tone.

The figure's head rises just above the far hill line into the glow while the torso reads against the mauve hills — a decent but not crisp silhouette that could read stronger if the hills dipped lower there. The figure faces right toward the moon and sits almost exactly at the horizontal center of the composition, which slightly divides the scene, though its small size softens that effect.

Looking at the right side now — it's mostly plain, lagoon, and moon, with the dark hill mass and tree weighted left, in a classic Friedrich asymmetry. The emptiness on the right feels intentional rather than a flaw, though the plain itself lacks structure; I notice there are already faint dark streaks and wisps near the horizon on the right that might serve as the thin violet stratus band I'd planned.

content.thinking:
Looking at the trunk base, I notice the root flare area reads more like two lighter brown mounds than actual roots, and the hill crest cuts horizontally behind the trunk in a way that makes the tree look pasted onto the hilltop rather than growing from it.

The fix is to darken the roots to match the trunk/hill tone so they merge into one silhouette mass, spreading them along the crest line with a few knuckles for grip. The hill's crest is also too smooth and uniform — it needs some unevenness like tussocks, a stone, or heather silhouettes against the light near the figure's and tree's feet, echoing the texture Friedrich uses in similar compositions.

Checking the figure's scale against the tree, the trunk diameter roughly matches the figure's height, implying a massive old oak with a ~1.75m trunk and ~16.7m height — plausible for a monumental ancient tree in Friedrich's style, and the figure's distance from the trunk of about 5m still feels reasonable. The separation between figure and tree also works thematically, since the figure stands on the crest between the tree and the view, looking outward, similar to how Friedrich places solitary figures near but not touching his trees in works like "Two Men Contemplating the Moon."

One issue though: the far hill line crosses right through the figure's neck and shoulders, creating an awkward tangent against the glow instead of the head and shoulders reading cleanly against the brightest sky, which is the effect Friedrich typically achieves and what I intended. I should either raise the figure onto a slightly higher point or dip the far hills behind him so his head and shoulders both sit silhouetted against the glow rather than just the head.

Repainting over the hills risks a visible patch since the sky_fix already left a raised seam there, so maybe it's simpler to just leave the figure-hill contrast as is since it reads fine — the real issue is the horizon tangent chopping the figure at the neck, which the dip would fix. I'll flag the dip as the recommended option and move on to checking the middle distance plain.

As for whether the plain convinces as space — the warm-to-olive gradient gives some atmospheric recession, but there's no structural perspective cues like diminishing hedgerows or banding to measure distance by. The two tree copses are the only objects there, and they're flawed: too dark for their distance, identically shaped with flat ruler-straight bottoms, and the left one floats oddly in the middle of the plain like a stray cloud shadow rather than sitting convincingly on the ground.

For fixes, I'd lighten both copses toward the haze value, break up their bottom edges so they settle into the terrain, and add a few horizontal bands of varying value across the plain — like field strips or heather patches, spaced tighter near the horizon — the way Friedrich handles similar flat landscapes.

I'm also thinking about repeating the thin water sliver motif at a couple more distances, getting progressively thicker and dimmer closer to the viewer, to help establish depth steps across the plain without overdoing it.

The near ground at the bottom right matches the hill's dark value, reading as a second ridge with a straight shelf-like top edge running across — this gives the picture's bottom a heavy dark band across its full width, consistent with Friedrich's tonal structure. The lagoon itself is the brightest strip in the land, running a consistent narrow width with straight edges, convincingly distant water, though I notice its left end tapers rather neatly.

Its left tip sits right next to the figure's stick, forming a long straight band running out the right edge like an arrow pulling the eye away from the composition. I also notice three parallel horizontals stacking up — the hill top, hill base, and lagoon edges — which is a device Friedrich used, but the lagoon's perfectly straight, constant width risks feeling too ribbon-like unless broken by something like a spit of land.

I want to vary its width with reeds, a darker island shape, and dim the far end, while keeping the water's brightness consistent with the sky glow reflected above the horizon. There are also stray specks on the plain and a bright mark near the right edge that need cleaning up, and the faint scumbled stratus bits in the sky currently read as dirt rather than clouds — I should either commit to real thin violet-gray stratus bands or remove them entirely.

Leaning toward adding two thin, tapering horizontal stratus bands low on the right, close in value to the sky but slightly darker with warmer lit lower edges, positioned below the moon's height and not crossing behind it, to give a gentle horizontal counterpoint to the tree.

I'm pulling together my overall assessment: the composition reads well with its dark hill mass, oak silhouette, figure, distant plain, lagoon, spire, and moon, and the sky-to-land value contrast works nicely. That uniform corrugated texture also contradicts Friedrich's thin, smooth painting method. The foreground lacks the usual tussocks, stones, or incidental details he'd use for scale, and the hill's shape — a perfectly round, symmetrical dome lit flatly — reads more like a burial mound than a heath, though a smooth dome could work as a repoussoir if handled differently.

I'm also noticing a mechanical quality to the hill's contour: a clean, almost geometric arc with a straight diagonal flank and a seam-like horizontal band where the plain meets the hill at the lower right. The plain itself has a soft, mottled texture that darkens slightly downward, which reads as plausible haze, but to the right of the hill it turns into a flat, uniform olive tone that breaks the illusion of atmospheric depth.

The middle stretch of plain also lacks any structure—no channel, hedges, or paths—leaving only a single copse that's roughly the same size and value as the distant clump near the horizon, which undermines the sense of recession since the farther object should read smaller and fainter. I'm thinking the mid-plain needs some horizontal element to establish scale and distance.

I'm also noticing a stray bright light-blue speck near the right edge at roughly x~995, y~557, which looks like a leftover accident from the failed channel attempt rather than an intentional element, and it's distracting since it sits right at the canvas edge where the eye catches it.

Checking proportions: the figure is roughly 6% of canvas height, about a third of the trunk-to-first-fork height, which works out to plausible human-to-oak scale for a big old tree — assuming the figure stands around 130 units away from the trunk.

In Friedrich's Rückenfigur compositions figures are often small and still read clearly (like Monk by the Sea), so the scale itself isn't the problem. The issue is the figure's silhouette competes with the massive trunk and gets visually absorbed into it since they share the same value — it should function as the compositional hinge instead.

Looking at the figure's gaze direction toward the moon and lagoon, that relationship works well; it's positioned right at the crest edge rather than lower on a shoulder, which is fine. The costume details — a tricorn-like cap, a touch of blue highlight on the coat — read clearly too.

The right stub on the trunk reads as a smooth, rounded peg rather than a jagged, splintered break, and the crown spreads too evenly, lacking Friedrich's angular, knotty asymmetry.

Looking closer, Friedrich's dead oaks are typically stag-headed — bare, antler-like dead limbs poking above a still-living lower crown — but this painting's claw-like twigs are too uniform and repetitive, plus the hooked, downward-curling sub-shoots on the lower left look more like seaweed tentacles than the straight, angular growth real oak limbs would show. Notes for the painter, day 56: answers to your four questions and what I'd change

The large shapes already work. The light sky against the dark land reads right away. The dusk gradient from smalt down to cream is the best passage in the picture, and the day-16 restatement left the zenith calm with no seam. The little spire is well judged: small and hazy, the same value as the far hills. Most of what I'd change is in the land and the tree. Here it is in order of importance, with your four questions answered along the way.

**1. The middle plain: the copses are what break the depth (your question 2).**
Look at the two copses in the value view: the one at x 640–720, y ~500, and the clump at x 890–1000, y ~490. They're the same value and both have hard edges, with bottoms cut flat as if by a ruler. The right one is nearer the horizon, so it's farther away, yet it isn't any lighter. Both are a good deal darker than the haze around them. That's why they look like cut-outs, small bushes a stone's throw off, when they should be woods a few kilometres away, and they flatten the plain around them.
- Scumble or glaze them toward the haze. The far clump should come close to the value of the far hills band. The nearer one can sit a step darker but still clearly lighter than the hill.
- Soften the bottom edges so they settle into the ground.

The plain itself (y 500–620) has a gentle gradient but nothing that recedes. Two things would build the space without any new objects:
- **Break up the lagoon.** At the horizon it's become one continuous strip of even thickness, from about x 520 to the right edge. In value it reads as a slit in the land, the ribbon problem again in a smaller form. Cut it into two or three lenses of different lengths, with low dark spits of land between them.
- **Add one nearer, larger water passage**, somewhere around y 540–570 on the right. Near water reflects higher sky, so make it a cooler, slightly bluer light than the cream far water. That warm-far, cool-near reflection is a strong depth cue, and it uses what you learned on day 13 (horizontal slivers, thin with distance).

There are already stray flecks there, ghosts of the old channel: x 880–980, y 530–570, and a light-blue speck right on the edge at x ~997, y ~555–565. Either build them into this pool or take them out. The one on the edge pulls the eye out of the frame.

**2. The figure (question 1).**
The scale is right, and its placement on the forward shoulder, apart from the trunk, is good. One fix: the far-hills contour runs across its neck at y ~456, so the head sits on the line. That tangency shrinks the figure, and the coat is set against the mid-grey hills instead of the glow you moved it for on day 6. Paint a shallow saddle into the far hills behind it, about 8–10 units deep over about 60 units of width, using your sky_fix glow mix. Then head and shoulders stand clear against the light. It's a small job with a big payoff, because the figure is the hinge of the picture.

**3. The oak (question 3): it reads as a fine dead tree, but not yet as an oak.**
Three things make it generic:
- **The trunk** is a parallel-sided column from y 480 to 360, like a post. Friedrich's oaks are squat and lumpy, with a swollen fork.
- **The crown** rises in a vase shape from a single fork. That's closer to an elm.
- **Every branch tip ends in the same motif:** a curled claw of two to four rigger hooks. On the far-left limb (x 80–130, y 250–300) they hang down like seaweed. That repetition is what gives the tree away as generic.

I wouldn't repaint it. Targeted changes:
- Break the trunk's contour with one or two bulges and a fuller fork. You can work from either side, cutting in with sky or adding tree paint.
- Put an abrupt kink into two of the main limbs, each with a short dead stub at the bend.
- Vary the tips. Leave some limbs ending blunt and broken, with nothing on them (stag-headed). Give only a few a dense, fine, angular mesh. Paint out the drooping curls.
- The right-hand stub at x 340–360, y 375 has a round, peg-like end. Shorten it and make the end splintered and jagged.

**4. The hill surface and shape.**
Look at the hill in the gallery and relief views. Because it's still wet, it may yet level, but right now it reads as a uniform crinkled leather: grey, wormy, with no direction. In raking light it also lifts the value, so the silhouette goes grey. It's the largest area in the picture, and the surface fights the glassy sky and the thin Friedrich method you planned. While it's still open, I'd do a flattening pass along the slope.

The contour is a near-perfect arc, like a burial mound. Where the crest crosses the lighter plain (x 230–460, and the right flank at 480–600), a few small breaks would loosen the arc and give the figure a scale reference: tussocks, a stone, a few heather tufts in silhouette. Also darken the hill slightly toward the bottom edge so the dome has some volume.

**5. The sky (question 4): yes to the cloud bands, but only low on the right, and only a few.**
Replace the stippled bits at x 680–830 and 900–1000, y 375–395. Up close they look like a halftone screen and don't match any other mark in the picture.
- Lay one or two long, thin, tapering bands parallel to the horizon, around y 385–415, using the calm ruler strokes that worked on day 16.
- Make them a violet-grey just darker than the glow.
- Keep them well clear of the moon and the zenith.

That also answers your other worry about the right side. It isn't too empty; emptiness suits this subject. What it needs is a little horizontal structure that echoes the horizon and carries the figure's gaze out to the moon. The bands and the reworked water do that without adding any objects.

**6. A small one for gallery light.**
The sky repair left of the trunk (x ~213–280, y ~375–403) shows as raised rectangles in relief and gallery light. You can't see it in flat view, but on a wall the square edges will show. If you can skim the ridges once it's hard, do; otherwise, keep any further patches soft-edged.

If you only have time for three of these, do the copse values, the saddle behind the figure, and the oak tips.
